# Optical Conductivity of a Single Hole in the Holstein-t-J Model

We employ dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) to investigate the optical conductivity of a single hole in the Holstein-t-J model. This theoretical framework provides a powerful approach for capturing the complex interplay between charge carriers, magnetic correlations, and lattice degrees of freedom that governs the transport properties of strongly correlated systems.

Within this approach, we derive an exact solution for the optical conductivity in the limit of infinite connectivity. This limit renders the DMFT treatment exact, allowing us to obtain rigorous results that serve as a benchmark for understanding the underlying physical mechanisms at play. By working in this well-controlled regime, we are able to disentangle the various contributions to the optical response with a high degree of precision.

We apply our analysis to the electron-doped cuprate compound Nd$_{2-x}$Ce$_x$CuO$_4$, a material of significant interest in the study of high-temperature superconductivity and correlated electron physics. This compound exhibits a rich optical conductivity spectrum whose interpretation has remained a subject of considerable debate.

Our results demonstrate that the Holstein-t-J model can successfully explain many of the salient features observed in the optical conductivity of this compound. The agreement between our theoretical predictions and the experimental observations lends strong support to the relevance of our model in describing the essential physics of this material.

Crucially, these features can be understood in terms of the formation of both magnetic and lattice polarons. The dressing of the hole by spin excitations of the antiferromagnetic background, combined with its coupling to lattice vibrations through the Holstein interaction, gives rise to composite quasiparticles whose signatures are directly reflected in the structure of the optical conductivity. This dual polaronic picture offers a unified and physically transparent interpretation of the experimental spectra.

# Optical Conductivity of a Single Hole in the Holstein-t-J Model: A Dynamical Mean-Field Study with Application to Nd$_{2-x}$Ce$_x$CuO$_4$

## Abstract

We employ dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) to investigate the optical conductivity of a single hole moving in an antiferromagnetic background coupled to lattice vibrations, as described by the Holstein-t-J model. By taking the limit of infinite connectivity, the many-body problem becomes exactly solvable, allowing us to obtain the full frequency dependence of the optical response without uncontrolled approximations. Applying this framework to the electron-doped cuprate Nd$_{2-x}$Ce$_x$CuO$_4$, we demonstrate that the model accounts for many of the salient features observed experimentally, which we interpret in terms of the formation of a composite magnetic/lattice polaron.

## Introduction and Motivation

The nature of charge carriers in doped Mott insulators remains one of the central questions in the physics of strongly correlated electron systems. In the cuprate high-temperature superconductors, a single carrier introduced into the antiferromagnetically ordered parent compound does not behave as a simple free particle. Instead, its motion is strongly dressed by two distinct sources of coupling: the surrounding spin fluctuations of the correlated background and the lattice degrees of freedom that respond to the local charge redistribution. The interplay between these magnetic and phononic contributions gives rise to a heavily renormalized quasiparticle—often described as a magnetic polaron or, when lattice effects are included, a magnetic/lattice polaron.

The optical conductivity provides a particularly sensitive probe of this polaronic physics. The distribution of spectral weight between a low-energy coherent (Drude-like) response and higher-energy incoherent absorption bands directly reflects how the carrier's kinetic energy is redistributed by its coupling to the surrounding medium. A quantitative theory of this response is therefore essential for disentangling the magnetic and lattice contributions to carrier dynamics.

## Model and Method

To capture both effects on equal footing, we consider the Holstein-t-J model, which combines the t-J Hamiltonian—describing the constrained hopping and antiferromagnetic exchange of correlated electrons—with a Holstein term representing the local coupling of the charge density to dispersionless optical phonons. This model encapsulates the essential competition and cooperation between spin-mediated and phonon-mediated polaron formation.

The full solution of such a model in finite dimensions is prohibitively difficult. However, in the limit of infinite lattice connectivity (equivalently, infinite spatial dimensions), dynamical mean-field theory becomes exact. In this limit, the self-energy becomes purely local, and the problem maps onto a self-consistently determined single-site problem embedded in an effective medium. This provides a controlled, non-perturbative treatment of the strong-coupling regime relevant to the polaron problem. Within this framework, we compute the single-particle spectral function and the current-current correlation function, from which the optical conductivity is obtained.

## Results and Application to Nd$_{2-x}$Ce$_x$CuO$_4$

Applying our analysis to the electron-doped cuprate Nd$_{2-x}$Ce$_x$CuO$_4$, we find that the calculated optical conductivity reproduces many of the characteristic features seen in experiment. In particular, the theory naturally yields:

- A transfer of optical spectral weight from high to low energies as the effective coupling strength is varied, consistent with polaronic renormalization of the carrier.
- Mid-infrared absorption bands whose position and width are governed by the combined magnetic exchange and electron-phonon coupling scales, reflecting the internal structure of the magnetic/lattice polaron.
- A suppression of the low-frequency coherent Drude weight relative to the non-interacting expectation, quantifying the mass enhancement of the dressed carrier.

The comparison indicates that the incoherent features of the optical spectra of Nd$_{2-x}$Ce$_x$CuO$_4$ cannot be attributed to either magnetic or lattice coupling alone. Rather, it is the cooperative dressing of the carrier by both spin fluctuations and phonons that reproduces the observed lineshapes and energy scales.

## Conclusion

By combining the Holstein-t-J model with an exact dynamical mean-field treatment in the infinite-connectivity limit, we provide a unified description of the optical conductivity of a single carrier in a correlated antiferromagnet coupled to the lattice. The successful account of the optical response of Nd$_{2-x}$Ce$_x$CuO$_4$ supports the picture that the low-energy charge dynamics of electron-doped cuprates are governed by the formation of a magnetic/lattice polaron, in which magnetic and phononic effects are intertwined. These results underscore the importance of treating spin and lattice degrees of freedom simultaneously when interpreting the spectroscopic properties of doped Mott insulators.

# Holstein Model and CuO: Understanding Electron-Phonon Coupling in Copper Oxides

## Introduction

The interplay between electrons and lattice vibrations plays a crucial role in determining the physical properties of many materials, particularly in copper oxide (CuO) compounds. The Holstein model provides a fundamental theoretical framework for understanding these electron-phonon interactions, which are essential for explaining phenomena ranging from polaron formation to potentially unconventional superconductivity.

## The Holstein Model

The Holstein model, introduced by Theodore Holstein in 1959, describes the coupling between electrons and localized (dispersionless) phonons. In its simplest form, the model considers electrons hopping between lattice sites while interacting with local vibrational modes. The key features include:

- **Electron hopping** between neighboring sites, characterized by a transfer integral
- **Local phonon modes** representing atomic or molecular vibrations
- **Electron-phonon coupling** that connects the electronic charge to the lattice displacement

When an electron moves through the lattice, it distorts the local environment, creating a "polaron"—a quasiparticle consisting of the electron dressed by its surrounding lattice deformation.

## Relevance to Copper Oxides

Copper oxide (CuO) and related cuprate compounds have attracted enormous scientific interest, particularly following the discovery of high-temperature superconductivity in these materials. The Holstein model becomes relevant in several ways:

### Polaron Physics
In CuO systems, the strong electron-phonon coupling can lead to the formation of polarons. These quasiparticles significantly affect charge transport properties and may contribute to the anomalous behavior observed in these materials.

### Structural Considerations
The copper-oxygen planes that characterize cuprate structures exhibit specific phonon modes. The oxygen atoms surrounding copper ions can vibrate in ways that couple strongly to the electronic degrees of freedom, making the Holstein framework a useful starting point for analysis.

## Applications and Extensions

While the pure Holstein model is a simplification, it serves as a foundation for more sophisticated theoretical treatments:

1. **Holstein-Hubbard Model**: Combines electron-phonon coupling with electron-electron correlations, essential for capturing the physics of strongly correlated cuprates.

2. **Bipolaron Theory**: Explores whether paired polarons could mediate superconducting behavior.

3. **Numerical Studies**: Modern computational methods, including quantum Monte Carlo and density matrix renormalization group techniques, allow detailed investigation of Holstein physics in realistic systems.

## Conclusion

The Holstein model remains an important theoretical tool for understanding the complex physics of copper oxides. While the complete picture of CuO-based materials requires accounting for strong electronic correlations and other effects, the fundamental insights provided by the Holstein model into electron-phonon coupling continue to inform research in condensed matter physics and materials science. Understanding these interactions is crucial for advancing our knowledge of superconductivity and other emergent phenomena in copper oxide systems.

# Abstract

The anomalous optical conductivity of electron-doped cuprate superconductors, characterized by mid-infrared absorption bands and a pronounced transfer of spectral weight upon doping, has long challenged conventional band-theory descriptions. Here we present a theoretical framework in which the coexistence of magnetic and lattice polaron formation self-consistently accounts for these spectral features. In the underdoped regime, doped electrons couple strongly to the antiferromagnetic spin background, dressing charge carriers into magnetic polarons whose incoherent motion generates a broad mid-infrared band displaced from the Drude peak. Concurrently, coupling to longitudinal optical phonons produces lattice polaron contributions that renormalize the effective carrier mass and introduce additional absorption structure at higher energies. We demonstrate that the interplay of these two dressing mechanisms determines the temperature and doping dependence of the optical spectral weight, reproducing the characteristic redistribution from low to intermediate frequencies as antiferromagnetic correlations weaken with increasing carrier concentration. The magnetic polaron component dominates near half-filling, where short-range spin order remains robust, while the lattice contribution grows in relative importance as the system approaches optimal doping and the coherent Drude response emerges. Our results reconcile the apparent violation of the f-sum rule within the low-energy manifold and clarify the distinct optical signatures separating electron-doped from hole-doped cuprates, notably the persistence of antiferromagnetism to higher doping levels on the electron side. These findings establish polaronic dressing as an essential ingredient for understanding charge dynamics in the proximity of the Mott-antiferromagnetic phase, with implications for the microscopic origin of superconducting pairing in the electron-doped family.
